title: The schools you met
hookLine: which way of practice drew you?

lines: A WALL, A BEAD, A FIELD AT NIGHT.
cards: A cushion in a Zen hall, facing a plain wall. Beads moving through fingers, one name at a time. A man alone in a field at night, talking to God in his own words.
A room of Quakers, quiet until someone is moved to speak. People in a park, moving slowly through the morning air. A table of Jewish students arguing over one line of text.
This year, the path toured the world's schools of practice, each on its own terms. Today, one question over the whole road. Not which way is best.
Which way, if any, drew you?

teach.h: A PULL IS NOT A RANKING.
teach.b: First, a pull is not a ranking. The schools aim at different ends: some at God, some at awakening, some at character, some at calm. Being drawn to a Zen wall says nothing against a Sufi circle.
It says something about you, today. Second, a pull is a place to start, not a proof.
In his first letter to the Thessalonians, Paul writes: "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Christians read that line in its own setting, inside the life of a church.
Taken plainly, it holds two moves: test first, then keep.
Zen, Tibetan Buddhism and some Hindu paths, as this path met them, stressed the teacher: a tug is where you start, and a good teacher and a community help you test it.
Third, a pull is an invitation, not a purchase. Some of what you met belongs inside a faith and its people. The Jesus Prayer lives in the prayer life of Orthodox Christians.
The Mevlevi turning is, for those who keep it, a ceremony of remembrance, not a performance. A pull toward one is an invitation to learn from its keepers, as a guest. Fourth, name the why.
The what is a practice; the why is a need.
Someone drawn to Quaker silence might be hungry for rest; someone drawn to kirtan, for company. A need can travel with you even when a practice can't, and naming it makes the next step easier to see.

how: People who explore several practices often keep a notebook of what drew them and why, then look for a teacher or a community in the tradition that keeps that practice, and learn from them as a guest.

games.q: after a year touring the world's schools of practice, one of them keeps pulling at you. what do you do first?
o: decide it's the best one and tell everyone.
write down why it drew you, then learn from the people who keep it.
ignore it; a pull means nothing.
games.why: today's lesson: the why names a need, and the people who keep a practice are where you learn it, as a guest. the pull is a start, not a verdict.

practice: Let the tour pass by like a slow train: the wall, the beads, the field, the silent room, the park, the study table, and notice which one stays in the window a moment longer; if none does, that's fine too.
If one does, ask quietly what in it pulls, the silence, the body moving, the words, the people. If you pray, you can bring the question into prayer.

wordCard.voice: The schools you met. Zen and insight, Tibetan, Christian, Jewish, Muslim and Sufi, Hindu, Sikh, Chinese and modern ways, each met in its own words and never ranked. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: drawn to. A pull is a beginning, never a verdict on anyone else's way. See you tomorrow.
